nameStory: Despite its common name, fen grass of Parnassus isn't actually a grass at all! The name comes from Mount Parnassus in Greece, home of the Muses in ancient mythology, where a related European species was first described. Early botanists thought its slender leaves resembled grass blades, leading to this wonderfully misleading name that has stuck for centuries.
description: Fen grass of Parnassus is a delicate wildflower that grows 6-16 inches tall in wet, boggy areas. It produces solitary white flowers with distinctive green or yellowish veins that sit atop slender stems. The plant has a small cluster of heart-shaped basal leaves at ground level, plus one distinctive stem leaf that clasps around the flower stalk partway up. This elegant little wildflower is actually quite rare and special to find in New England's wetlands.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single white flower per stem with 5 rounded petals marked by delicate green or pale yellow veins that look like tiny roadmaps. The flower faces upward and measures about an inch across with a sweet, subtle fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped basal leaves clustered at ground level feel smooth and slightly thick, plus one unique stem leaf that wraps completely around the flower stalk like a collar about halfway up.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant 6-16 inches tall with typically just one flower per plant on a single, slender stem rising from a rosette of leaves at the base.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops a small, egg-shaped capsule that splits open to release tiny seeds, often persisting into fall as a brown, papery structure.

habitat: Look for fen grass of Parnassus in calcareous (limestone-influenced) wetlands, fens, and boggy areas with consistent moisture. It thrives in alkaline soils and is often found alongside sedges, other bog plants, and sometimes near seepy areas in meadows. In New England, it's most commonly found in northern Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine where the right soil chemistry and wetland conditions exist.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as small heart-shaped rosettes close to the ground, bright green and smooth to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through August, when the distinctive white flowers with green veining are most visible and fragrant.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, turning brown and papery while basal leaves may persist with slight yellowing.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground parts, leaving no visible trace above ground until spring.

funFact: This plant was once believed to have magical properties and was used in medieval Europe to treat heart ailments, which may explain why its leaves are so perfectly heart-shaped - nature's own prescription label!
confusionNotes: The heart-shaped basal leaves might be confused with wild ginger or violet leaves when not in bloom, but the distinctive stem leaf that wraps around the flower stalk is unique. Remember: if there's a leaf hugging the stem like a collar, you've found grass of Parnassus.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - this isn't related to grasses at all, but belongs to the staff-vine family. It's also quite rare in New England, so if you find one, consider yourself lucky to witness this wetland treasure. The 'glauca' in its scientific name refers to its slightly blue-green leaf color.
compareHints: Fen grass of Parnassus is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique among our flora. Within the staff-vine family, it's quite different from its relatives like bittersweet, being a small herbaceous wildflower rather than a woody vine. Its combination of heart-shaped basal leaves, clasping stem leaf, and single white veined flower makes it unmistakable once you know what to look for.
